stories.title: How native seeds are mending Wyoming’s landscape
stories.summary: After years of collecting and growing native seeds in a Lander lab, The Nature Conservancy planted two acres of sagebrush and tansy aster at an abandoned Wyoming mine site. The goal: rebuild habitat for sage grouse and pronghorn, and prove native seeds can heal scarred land at scale.
stories.extended_summary: Twenty-five miles down a bumpy gravel road outside Jeffrey City, Wyoming, scientist Michaela Owens met contractors at an abandoned mine site to plant two acres of seeds she's studied for years. They came from The Nature Conservancy's seed lab in Lander, where native plants are collected, tested, and grown—and this planting is one of the organization's first large-scale reclamation projects. The state wants more sagebrush here to lift the ecosystem back to match the intact habitat around it, critical ground for sage grouse. Owens brought tansy aster too, and she's happy whenever pronghorn eat her plants. It's research turning into landscape, one seed at a time.

stories.title: Recovery without a scar: How a study on jellyfish eyes could revolutionize modern retinal care
stories.summary: Jellyfish can regrow damaged eyes—no scar tissue, fully functional—and their eyes have lenses, corneas, and retinas remarkably like ours. A UC Santa Cruz biologist just won a $2 million NIH grant to figure out how, with an eye toward future gene therapy for human retinal disease.
stories.extended_summary: When a jellyfish damages its eye, its cells don't form scar tissue—they regenerate a fully functional eye. That's the phenomenon evolutionary biologist Aide Macias-Muñoz wants to decode. Jellyfish ocular structures are remarkably similar to ours, with lenses, corneas, and retinas, and about 1 in 1,380 people worldwide suffer from inherited retinal diseases that human biology can't currently reverse. A recent $2 million NIH grant funds her UC Santa Cruz lab's study of box and moon jellyfish at different life stages, using single-cell sequencing to test how development and regeneration connect. The distant evolutionary ancestor might just teach us how to heal human vision.

stories.title: “Remember they resisted”: The artist painting bold, bright portraits of every queer Holocaust victim
stories.summary: Artist Bry Sharland is painting portraits of every photographed queer victim of the Nazi regime—about 65 done, possibly 700 to go. stories.extended_summary: Bry Sharland starts with a black-and-white intake photo or police mugshot—the worst moment of someone's life—and gives it color, and gives them their joy. His Pink Triangle Portraits project aims to paint every photographed queer victim of the Nazi regime: about 65 are finished, and he estimates up to 700 more could exist. Named for the badge forced on queer people in the camps and later reclaimed as a symbol of Pride, each portrait comes with as much of the subject's life story as Sharland can research. 'Remember they resisted,' the project insists—not just that they suffered, but who they were and how they lived.
